title: Economic Development Planning: Meaning, Aims and Types
summary: What economic planning is, its seven aims and the main types of plan.

p: Economic development planning is like drawing a roadmap for a country's future. It is the government's conscious effort to guide the economy towards chosen goals and to use resources wisely for fast and lasting growth.

Economic planning: the deliberate allocation of a nation's resources by the government to different sectors in order to reach specific economic goals. Development planning: the strategic mapping of the actions the government will take to achieve overall growth and development. A plan is a rational, systematic use of resources, with government influence, direction and control.

1. Increase employment. 2. Develop efficient technology. 3. Increase real income and living standards. 4. Allocate resources fairly across sectors and regions. 5. Diversify the economy away from a single sector such as oil. 6. Reduce income inequality. 7. Reduce foreign control by raising local ownership of the economy.
Study the table.

head: Type
Meaning
rows: Concerned with sharing out national income among sectors
Aimed at achieving a few specific, critical objectives
Sets targets for all the main sectors of the economy (for example Nigeria's five-year plans)
Covers only one part of the economy, such as agriculture or education
Common in socialist systems; the government controls both the making and the carrying out of plans

sections.h: Benefits of planning to a nation
p: It sets clear goals and priorities; avoids waste by using scarce resources where they matter most; creates jobs and reduces poverty in a purposeful way; makes it possible to measure progress; and attracts investors by making policy more predictable.

A plan goes through steps: set goals (for example job creation or diversification); formulate policies and strategies; implement the plan by allocating resources and carrying out projects; monitor and evaluate progress by collecting data; and use the feedback to adjust the plan. The picture of this cycle in your lesson note has a spelling error, so we describe it in words.

title: Nigeria's Planning Experience and Its Problems
summary: The national development plans from 1962 to NEEDS, and six reasons why planning has often failed.

p: 1st National Development Plan: 1962 to 1968. 2nd: 1970 to 1974 (after the civil war, focusing on reconstruction). 3rd: 1975 to 1980 (oil-boom years with very large spending). 4th: 1981 to 1985. Later came rolling plans, the National Economic Empowerment and Development Strategy (NEEDS) from 2003/2004, and Vision 20:2020 (you study these this term).

1. Political instability: frequent changes of government lead to inconsistent policy and abandoned projects. 2. Inadequate capital: not enough money for projects. 3. Shortage of skilled personnel: lack of technical experts, partly through brain drain. 4. Rapid population growth: can outpace economic growth and strain resources. 5. Insufficient data: poor statistics cause wrong forecasts. 6. Poor implementation and cost overruns: projects are badly executed and costs exceed estimates. Add: corruption, and over-dependence on oil income, which makes budgets uncertain.

A road is planned at ₦10 billion over three years. The government changes in year two, the new government prefers another project, funds are diverted, and the road is left half built. Costs rise by 40% from inflation. This shows political instability, poor implementation and cost overruns together.
Political will and continuity across governments; reliable data; a skilled civil service; honest management of funds; the involvement of states, firms and citizens; and regular review.

title: The International Monetary Fund (IMF)
summary: The IMF's origin, aims, quota system, criticisms and benefits to Nigeria.

p: In a connected world, nations form economic organisations to deal with common problems, increase trade and promote stability.

sections.h: The IMF: the global financial firefighter
p: Founded in 1944 at the Bretton Woods Conference in New Hampshire, USA (it began operations soon after). Headquarters: Washington, D.C. Membership: about 190 countries. Main goal: the stability of the international monetary system, that is the system of exchange rates and payments that lets countries trade with each other.

img.alt: Two panels showing the IMF's dual role: a firefighter putting out a balance of payments crisis as emergency response, and a doctor checking a globe as prevention through policy advice and monitoring
img.cap: The IMF as firefighter and doctor.

p: 1. Promote international monetary cooperation. 2. Encourage balanced growth of trade, which supports jobs and incomes. 3. Promote exchange rate stability. 4. Lend temporarily to members with balance of payments problems. 5. Give technical help and training.

Each member pays a quota based on the size of its economy. The quota decides its voting power (the USA, Japan and Germany have more votes), how much it can borrow, and its share of Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), an international reserve asset created by the IMF.

Strict conditions (conditionality), often called structural adjustment programmes (SAPs), may require cuts in spending on health and education and the privatisation of state assets, which can cause hardship. Dominance of rich nations in voting. A 'one-size-fits-all' approach that does not fit local conditions.

sections.h: Benefits to Nigeria and West Africa
p: Support in a balance of payments crisis, for example after an oil price crash; policy credibility, because an IMF programme tells investors that a country is serious about sound policy; and data, assessments and advice.

sections.h: Why might a country hesitate to borrow from the IMF?
p: Because of the conditions: cutting subsidies, devaluing the currency, reducing public spending and privatising state firms are often unpopular and can hurt the poor in the short term; and a loan may also be seen as a loss of independence.

title: The World Bank and How It Differs from the IMF
summary: The aims of the World Bank, its benefits to Nigeria and a comparison with the IMF.

p: The World Bank (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, IBRD) was also founded in 1944 at Bretton Woods and has its headquarters in Washington, D.C. It is the IMF's sister organisation but with a different job: to reduce poverty and support long-term development by financing and advising on specific projects.

1. Finance reconstruction and development: roads, dams, power plants. 2. Promote foreign investment by guaranteeing loans. 3. Support sustainable development in education, health and the environment. 4. Provide technical expertise and research.
Study the table.

IMF

rows: Short-term economic stability and macroeconomic problems

p: Infrastructure: the Bank has supported roads, hydroelectric and power projects and rural water schemes. Your lesson note names the Lagos-Ibadan expressway; check this against your teacher's notes, because many roads have been financed from several sources. Human capital: funding for education and health, including campaigns against malaria and polio. Reconstruction: loans to help rebuild after the civil war.

sections.h: Primary roles in one sentence each
p: IMF: lender and adviser that keeps the international payments system stable and helps countries with short-term balance of payments crises. World Bank: lender and adviser that finances long-term development projects to reduce poverty.

title: ECOWAS: The Economic Community of West African States
summary: The founding, aims, institutions, achievements and problems of ECOWAS, with a note on recent changes in membership.

p: ECOWAS was founded on 28 May 1975 by the Treaty of Lagos. Its headquarters is in Abuja, Nigeria. It had 15 member states. Note: in January 2025 Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger left the community, so it now has 12 members. Its main goal is economic integration and cooperation in West Africa.

1. Create a free trade area by removing customs duties and barriers among members. 2. Build a common market with free movement of people, goods, services and capital. 3. Harmonise agricultural, economic, monetary and industrial policies. 4. Promote peace and security through collective mechanisms.

Authority of Heads of State and Government (the highest decision-making body); the ECOWAS Commission (administration); the Community Parliament (discussion); the Community Court of Justice (explains the treaty and settles disputes); and the ECOWAS Bank for Investment and Development (EBID), which finances projects.

The ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme (ETLS) for tariff-free movement of certain goods. The ECOWAS passport and visa-free travel for up to 90 days. ECOMOG, the ceasefire monitoring group that intervened in Liberia and Sierra Leone. Cooperation in health (fighting epidemics), sports and security.

Similar economies: many members export similar raw materials such as cocoa, oil and cotton, so they compete instead of trading with each other. Poor infrastructure and slow border posts. Many currencies: the CFA franc (used by some) and the naira, cedi and others, which complicates monetary union (the planned 'eco' currency has been delayed). Political instability: coups and crises in some states. Border closures and non-tariff barriers.
Two achievements: free movement of people (visa-free travel) and peacekeeping (ECOMOG). Two challenges: the similarity of the members' economies, and political instability or poor infrastructure.

title: The African Development Bank and UNCTAD
summary: The AfDB and UNCTAD: their founding, goals, functions and importance for developing countries.

p: Africa's home-grown development fund. Founded in 1964; headquarters Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire. Membership: 81 states (54 African and 27 non-African). Primary goal: to spur sustainable economic development and social progress in its African member countries.

Objectives: 1. Loans and grants for agriculture, health, education and infrastructure. 2. Mobilise public and private investment into Africa. 3. Policy advice and research. 4. Promote regional integration through cross-border projects such as roads and power pools.

Why it matters: it is African-led and understands African problems; it invests in 'soft' infrastructure (education, health) as well as 'hard' infrastructure (roads, power); and it encourages private firms to invest by funding risky projects.

The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development was set up in 1964 as a permanent organ of the UN General Assembly. Headquarters: Geneva, Switzerland. Primary goal: to help developing countries join the world economy fairly.

Objectives: 1. Make world trade rules development-friendly. 2. Help countries that depend on a few raw materials to diversify (commodity dependence). 3. Support debt management. 4. Analyse globalisation. It is a think-tank (the Trade and Development Report) and a forum where developing countries can speak out.

sections.h: AfDB and the World Bank compared
p: Both lend for development. The AfDB lends to African countries and is owned mainly by African members; the World Bank is global. The AfDB's focus is on African integration and projects; the World Bank's scope is wider.
AfDB financing for power, roads and agriculture projects and support for private investment; UNCTAD's research and advice on diversifying away from oil and on trade policy.

activity: Write short notes on the AfDB and UNCTAD (year founded, headquarters, goal and two objectives each). Explain why an African-led bank may be better placed to understand African problems.

title: OPEC: The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
summary: The founding, aims, quotas, achievements and challenges of OPEC and how it affects Nigeria.

p: OPEC was founded in 1960 in Baghdad by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. Its headquarters is in Vienna, Austria. Nigeria joined in 1971. The lesson note says it has 13 members; in recent years some members have left (for example Angola in 2024), so it now has fewer, about 12. A 'cartel' is a group of producers that agree to control output and price.

img.alt: A balance with oil supply on one side and consumer demand on the other, held by a hand, to show OPEC balancing supply and demand

p: 1. Price stability: avoid harmful swings in oil prices. 2. A steady supply of petroleum to consumers. 3. A fair return for producers who invest in oil. 4. Production quotas to manage world supply.
By agreeing to cut or raise production together. If members cut output, supply falls and prices tend to rise; if they raise output, prices tend to fall.
Higher prices and more control over oil resources for members in the 1970s; a major role in world politics and economics; a hub of information and analysis on the oil market.

Quota cheating: members produce more than their quota for short-term income. Political rivalry, for example between Saudi Arabia and Iran. Rise of non-OPEC producers such as the USA (shale oil), Russia and Brazil. The energy transition to renewable energy, which may reduce long-term demand for oil.

Nigeria's quota limits how much it may sell, and its revenue depends on the oil price that OPEC decisions influence. Quota limits, theft and pipeline damage have sometimes left Nigeria producing below its quota, which cuts income.

title: The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)
summary: The eight goals, what Nigeria achieved, why most were not met and how the story continues with the SDGs.

p: The MDGs were eight international development targets set after the UN Millennium Summit in 2000, when world leaders, including Nigeria's, promised to cut extreme poverty and improve human development by 2015.

sections.h: The eight goals and Nigeria's record
p: Study the table. These assessments follow your lesson note and are summaries.

head: Goal
Aim
Nigeria's performance
rows: Halve the share of people living on less than $1.25 a day and those who suffer hunger
Largely not met; growth did not much reduce poverty
Partly met; enrolment rose but quality, dropout and infrastructure remained problems
3. Gender equality and empowerment of women
Moderate progress; the gap narrowed but women were under-represented in politics and senior jobs
Not met, though immunisation brought improvement
Not met; Nigeria remained among the worst in the world
6. Combat HIV/AIDS, malaria and other diseases
Good progress; HIV prevalence fell and malaria control grew
Mixed; deforestation, pollution and poor access to water and sanitation remained
Open, fair trade and financial system; debt relief
Ongoing; debt and trade imbalances persisted

p: The MDGs focused attention and resources on health and education, but Nigeria missed most targets. Reasons: weak implementation, corruption, too little funding and a lack of reliable data to track progress.
In 2015 the world adopted the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), 17 goals to be met by 2030, which are wider than the MDGs and include climate action, clean energy and strong institutions.
